progression.startsWith: Carbon-13 told you ethanol has two kinds of carbon. Now look at its proton NMR spectrum. There are three signals, they're different sizes, and two of them are split into little clusters of lines. Each of those features is a separate clue. Read all three, and the spectrum tells you not just which hydrogens are there, but how they're joined.
progression.stopsAfter: counting hydrogen environments; reading a given shift; using areas as a ratio scaled by the formula; explaining and applying the n+1 rule, with the O–H and equivalence limits; reading and predicting a whole spectrum; the ethyl and lone CH₃ patterns.
progression.nextLesson: combining MS, IR and NMR (route chem-m8-c12).

teaching.task: Carbon-13 told you ethanol has two kinds of carbon. Its proton spectrum shows three signals, of different sizes, and two are split. What does each feature tell you?
teaching.causalExplanation: (1) the proton spectrum shows three features, each a clue (1); (2) same shielding idea, 0 to 12 ppm, shifts given in the question (2); (3) hydrogens in identical surroundings share a signal; symmetry merges them; ethanol three (3); (4) the CH₂ next to oxygen is deshielded, so further left (4); (5) area is proportional to the number of hydrogens; integration line; areas, not heights; a ratio, not the numbers (5); (6) neighbouring hydrogens add to or subtract from the field, so two neighbours give three lines (6); (7) n+1; who counts as a neighbour; O–H singlet (7); (8) bromoethane read from scratch (8); (9) a quartet is not four hydrogens (9); (10) ethyl ethanoate: the lone CH₃ singlet and the ester oxygen (10); memory aid (11); attempts (12 to 15); decision rule and handoff (16); key notes (17).
teaching.conversationalApproach: Carbon-13 told you ethanol has two kinds of carbon. Proton NMR works the same way as carbon-13, but it watches hydrogen-1 nuclei, called protons here. First clue: the number of signals. Second, where each signal sits. Third, how big each signal is. Now the clusters of lines. That's the n plus one rule. Let's read one from scratch. Here's the classic trap. Now a molecule with a surprise. One line for the three clues: signals, areas, neighbours plus one. Your turn. Three signals, in the ratio three to two to three. Last one. It's pentan-3-one. So, with a proton spectrum, ask four questions.

teaching.understandingCheck: (A1) "Predict the ¹H NMR spectrum of methyl propanoate, CH₃CH₂COOCH₃. State the number of signals, their relative areas and the splitting of each signal. Justify your answer." Answer: three signals, 3 : 2 : 3; OCH₃ singlet (no hydrogens on the next atom; the oxygen carries none); CH₂ quartet (three neighbours on the CH₃); CH₃ triplet (two neighbours on the CH₂). Crossed mistake: "CH₂ is a sextet: counted the OCH₃ hydrogens too" (hydrogens across the C=O and the ester oxygen are not on the next carbon). (A2) "A compound with molecular formula C₅H₁₀O is one of: pentan-2-one, pentan-3-one, pentanal, 3-methylbutan-2-one. Its ¹H NMR spectrum shows two signals: a triplet at 1.05 ppm with relative area 3, and a quartet at 2.44 ppm with relative area 2. (A CH₂ next to a C=O group appears at about 2.0 to 2.7 ppm.) Identify the compound. Justify your answer using the number of signals, the relative areas and the splitting." Answer: pentan-3-one; triplet and quartet in 3 : 2 is an ethyl pattern; ten hydrogens make the real numbers 6 and 4, so two identical ethyl groups; two signals mean symmetry; the 2.44 quartet fits CH₂ beside the C=O; the others give four, five and three signals. Crossed mistake: "3 : 2 means five hydrogens, so one ethyl group".

design.visualSystem: the NMR machine and the sample tube as painted plates listed by filename (both from c11a), never stretched; spectra are coded diagrams only (c11a's NmrSpectrum component in proton mode), with realistic shifts for the named compounds, never AI images; molecules come from the coded molecule kit (src/explainer/lessons/chem-m7-c01/molecules.tsx), drawn with their hydrogens where hydrogens are the subject, each hydrogen environment ringed in the same colour as its signal; nuclear magnets coded as abstract arrows; no people, hands or faces; at most about three bright text items, earlier lines dim; one reasoning stage at a time; "Pause here to answer." then a 10 s countdown with the full worded question kept on screen; no givens card, givens underlined in the feedback as they are used; brief feedback (answer, key reason, one crossed mistake, about 15 to 30 s); original HSC-style questions only; Australian spelling; no em dashes; conversational narration; no absolute claims ("usually", "fits").
